subject: physics_2
question_text: Which needle is to be used at the poles?

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: at the magnetic poles the dip is 90° and the horizontal component is zero, so a horizontal compass reads nothing useful; a dip needle — a magnetised needle pivoted to turn in a vertical plane containing the earth's field — is what reads there, standing vertical at dip 90°. The book's question wording 'Which needle to be used at poles ?' is completed grammatically here without changing what is asked.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The dip needle
lines: A dip needle is used at the poles.
A dip needle is a magnetised needle
pivoted to turn in a vertical plane that
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the instrument and say what it is — a needle pivoted in a vertical plane.
steps.why: The answer is an instrument choice, so the mark needs the instrument named and defined. The defining feature is the pivot: vertical plane, not horizontal.
common_mistakes: Answering an ordinary compass. A compass turns in the horizontal plane and is the needle that fails at the poles.
Naming the dip needle without saying it turns in a vertical plane — the pivot plane is the definition.

recall.must_convey: That a dip needle is used — a magnetised needle pivoted to turn in a vertical plane containing the earth's field.
accept: turns in the vertical plane of the field
reject: the field is vertical at the poles

steps.memory_tip: The dip needle measures dip, so it must be free to tilt — its pivot lets it swing in a vertical plane.

steps.label: Why it works there
lines: At the poles the earth's field is vertical,
so the dip needle stands vertical and
A compass that turns only in the
horizontal plane shows no direction there,
because the horizontal component is zero.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Contrast the two needles: the dip needle reads 90°; the flat compass reads nothing.
steps.why: The instrument must be able to follow the field's direction. At the poles the field is vertical, and only a needle free to tilt can line up with it — the dip needle does, and its 90° reading is itself the measurement.
common_mistakes: Saying the dip needle points north at the poles. It stands vertical — its reading there is 90°, not a horizontal direction.
Giving the field-is-vertical fact without connecting it to the needle's pivot plane.

recall.must_convey: That the field at the poles is vertical, so the dip needle stands vertical reading 90° while a horizontal compass shows nothing.
accept: reads ninety degrees at the poles
the horizontal compass shows no direction

steps.memory_tip: Match the pivot to the field: vertical field at the poles needs the needle that can tilt vertical.

insider_note: At the poles the field is vertical, so a compass needle pivoted in the horizontal plane has no direction to settle on. The dip needle, free to turn in a vertical plane, is the one that lines up with the field, and it reads 90°.
